 Social Security's 3.6% Raise for 2027 Could Shrink Once a Projected $6.60 Medicare Part B Increase Is Deducted
 Published Oct 18, 2026 10:25 PM EDT 
 By
 Dorothy Brooks 
 Andrew Harnik | Getty Images 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on Pocket 
 Social Security beneficiaries will get a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) in 2027, the Social Security Administration announced Oct. 14. The raise adds about $75 a month to the average retirement benefit, but a projected Medicare Part B increase could take part of that back.
 The 2027 Part B figures are still projections from the Medicare Trustees. Under those projections, the standard Part B premium would rise from $202.90 to $209.50 a month in 2027. For most retirees, that premium comes straight out of their Social Security check, so the real raise depends on both numbers.
 The Math for a Typical Retiree
 The raise reaches nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries starting in January 2027. About 7.3 million people who receive Supplemental Security Income will see their increase Dec. 31, 2026. The COLA gives beneficiaries "greater financial stability," Social Security Commissioner Frank J. Bisignano said.
 The average retirement benefit will rise from $2,095 to $2,170 a month, according to the SSA's 2027 COLA fact sheet from Social Security . For an average retiree, a $75 monthly increase minus a $6.60 premium increase would leave about $68 more per month, if the projected premium holds. That works out to roughly $820 more over the year, compared with $900 before the premium change. Individual amounts will vary.
 The annual Part B deductible is also projected to rise, from $283 to $292, according to AARP's review of the trustees' figures . That means slightly higher out-of-pocket costs before Medicare starts paying its share of doctor visits, outpatient care, and many tests.
 MedicalDaily previously reported that Part B could rise to $209.50 in 2027 before the raise was known. With the COLA now set at 3.6%, retirees can estimate their net change with more confidence, though the final premium could still differ.
 The 2027 increase is far smaller than this year's jump. The 2026 standard premium rose $17.90, or 9.7%, from $185, according to CMS's 2026 Part B premium and deductible fact sheet .
 Who Feels the Squeeze Most
 Not everyone pays the standard premium. Higher-income beneficiaries pay an extra charge, known as the income-related monthly adjustment amount (IRMAA), based on tax returns from two years earlier. About 5.1 million people paid that surcharge in 2025, according to AARP.
 A rule known as hold harmless protects many retirees from seeing their Social Security payment drop when Part B rises. But about 30% of Part B enrollees are not covered by it, including people who do not receive Social Security checks and those who pay IRMAA.
 The pinch is sharpest for retirees on fixed incomes with high medical needs. People who see specialists often, need outpatient procedures, or take expensive drugs may find that rising deductibles, copays, and drug costs absorb much of the COLA. Caregivers managing a parent's budget should watch for those combined costs.
 Longer-term pressure on Medicare is also building. The trustees project that the Hospital Insurance trust fund, which pays for Part A hospital care, will be depleted in the second quarter of 2033, according to the 2026 Medicare Trustees Report . At that point, incoming revenue would cover 89% of costs unless Congress acts.
 Steps Retirees Can Take Before 2027
 Watch for your official notice. Social Security will post COLA notices in my Social Security starting in late November, and Medicare enrollees can see their 2027 premium in the Message Center at that time. People must sign up for paperless notices by Nov. 18 to see them online. Everyone else will get a notice by mail in December.
 Use Medicare open enrollment, which runs Oct. 15 through Dec. 7. Comparing Medicare Advantage and Part D drug plans can make a bigger difference than the Part B premium itself, especially for people with high drug costs. Free counseling is available through State Health Insurance Assistance Programs.
 Low-income beneficiaries should ask about Medicare Savings Programs , which can help pay Part B premiums and other costs, and about Extra Help for prescription drugs. Eligibility depends on income and assets, and state Medicaid offices handle Medicare Savings Program applications.
 People paying IRMAA whose income has dropped because of retirement, divorce, or a spouse's death can ask Social Security to reconsider the surcharge. Keeping documentation of the life change speeds the process.
 Budget for health costs separately from the raise. Writing down expected premiums, deductibles, and regular copays can show whether the COLA covers rising expenses or whether adjustments are needed.
 The main uncertainty is the final premium. CMS typically announces Part B rates in the fall, and the actual figure could be higher or lower than the trustees' projection. Until then, retirees should plan on keeping somewhat less than $75 a month once Medicare costs are counted.

 Key Questions Answered
 How big is the 2027 Social Security raise? A 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment, about $75 a month for the average retiree.
 How much is Part B expected to rise? From $202.90 to a projected $209.50 a month, an increase of $6.60.
 What is the net raise after Part B? About $68 a month for an average retiree, if the projection holds.
 Is the 2027 Part B premium final? No. CMS will announce final rates later this fall.
 When will people see their new amounts? Online in my Social Security starting in late November, or by mail in December.
 Where can low-income retirees get help? Medicare Savings Programs and Extra Help, through state Medicaid offices and Social Security.
